 Judgment

1. Revisionist namely Kartar Singh has filed present revision petition, thereby challenging order dated 14.10.2023, passed by Ld. Trial Court in Complaint Case No. 702/2023, vide which, Ld. Trial Court had allowed the application of complainant Krishan, u/sec. 156 (3) CrPC and ordered for registration for FIR.

sentences.text: In my subsequent paragraphs, parties will be referred with the same nomenclature with which they were referred before Ld. Trial Court, in order to avoid confusion.
3. Trial Court record reveal that complainant Krishan had filed an application u/sec. 156(3)CrPC against accused persons, praying for registration of FIR, before Ld. Trial Court.

The allegations in the complaint are mentioned below :-
"That accused Kartar R/o Village Madanpur Khadar, New Delhi- 110076, is a man of criminal antecedents and has breached the trust of complainants namely Krishan,
Mahipal and Jaipali.

It is further stated that accused was friend of late father of complainant and due to unfortunate death of father of the complainant in the year 2006-2007 his family is facing financial crises for which complainant no. 3 contacted the accused Kartar and asked for a loan on pretext of CR No. 625/2023 2 of 11 Kartar Singh Vs. Krishan & Ors.
which complainant(s) took loans from accused Kartar on various occasions (Rs.
20,000/- to 50,000/-) on interest but on every occasion complainant(s) paid back the loan amount with interest on time to the accused.

It is further stated that on account of loans, complainant(s) gave a surety to the accused for which accused took thumb prints of complainant no. 3 on a blank paper and kept those papers in his possession.

The accused was well aware that father of the complainant no. 1 was in possession of agriculture land admeasuring 2 acre in Village Jaitpur Khadda Colony and as per the revenue records, said land was in possession of the father of complainant no. 1 which was being cultivated by father of complainant for his livelihood.
It is further stated that accused was well aware about the fact that father of complainant Late Sh. Balraj was not the owner of the said land.

Complainant came to know about the execution of false documents by forging the thumb print of complainant no. 3 and signatures of complainant no. 2 and 3 when they received a notice to join enquiry by the police officials.

Complainants were never aware about the forged signatures or documents as the accused had never taken any legal action or never sued complainants CR No. 625/2023 3 of 11 Kartar Singh Vs. Krishan & Ors.
in any civil matter for the possession of aforesaid property on the basis of said documents.

It is further stated that complainant no. 3 is illiterate lady and was also not aware about any such agreement to transfer the property and she was only aware about the monetary transactions between the complainant no. 3.

Thereafter,
complainant gave a written complaint to the police and also to the other higher authorities but neither the action has been taken nor FIR was lodged.

Based on said claims, complainant prayed that FIR be registered against accused persons u/sec.417/420/406/467/468/471/120B IPC."
4.

In the ATR report filed by SHO PS- Kalindi Kunj, it is stated that due inquiry was conducted and it was stated by the complainant that he had taken a friendly loan from the accused persons and the complainant had entered into some agreement with the accused persons but had mentioned that Kartar Singh vs Krishan And Ors on 16 February, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/102832952/
2 they were only the cultivators in possession of the land and were not the owners of the said land.

sentences.text: IO had stated that the owner of the aforesaid land as per the revenue department is Akil Mohd. and had further stated that alleged complainants Mahipal and Krishan were not aware about the aforesaid agreement between the complainant and the accused persons.

Complainant Jaipali had informed the IO that she had only taken a friendly loan from the accused and she also did not gave any satisfactory reply with regard to the aforesaid agreement.
CR No. 625/2023 4 of 11 Kartar Singh Vs. Krishan & Ors.
Further, complainant was also inquired and has stated that same facts as mentioned in his complaint.
IO further submitted that an FIR No. 397/2014 u/sec. 420/467/468/471/120B IPC has already been registered at PS Jaitpur on the complaint of Manoj Malik qua the abovesaid land.

5. Ld. Trial Court after considering the contents of application u/sec. 156(3) CrPC and the said action taken report, allowed the application of the complainant vide impugned order dated 14.10.2023 and ordered for registration of FIR.
6.
In the revision petition, complainant claimed that Ld. Trial Court did not pass proper legal order as it disregarded the law, laid down by higher courts.

Revisionist has challenged the impugned order on the grounds that the Ld. Trial Court had failed to appreciate that the revisionist had been cheated for a sum of Rs. 92,50,000/- and the complainant failed to give any satisfactory reply to the IO which is also mentioned in the ATR report.

Further, the land in question as per the revenue record,
is owned by one Akil Mohd.
Further, that the Ld. Trial Court did not take into consideration facts inquired upon by the IO.
Further, Ld. Trial Court overlooked the status report and that the matter did not require police investigation as a civil litigation is pending between the parties.

Further, the complainant had already admitted that they had received an amount of Rs. 92,50,000/- from the revisionist and therefore, the impugned order dated 14.10.2023, is liable to set aside.
CR No. 625/2023 5 of 11 Kartar Singh Vs. Krishan & Ors.
7.

Per contra, Ld. Counsel for respondents herein has argued that impugned order passed by Ld.
Trial Court was legally correct and needs no interference.
As per the complaint, the allegations against the accused persons are pertaining to forgery which could not have been investigated by the complainant without assistance of the police officials.

Further, that the accused Jaipali (being the complainant before the Trial Court) is poor uneducated old lady and she was not aware regarding the intention of the accused persons and had always told the accused persons that she was only having possession of the land being the cultivator.

It is further argued that the accused persons/
revisionist herein, had played fraud upon the complainant by forging the documents.

Further, all the facts alleged were not within the knowledge and possession of the respondents (being the complainant before Ld. Trial Court) and there was need for investigation after registration of FIR to unearth the contentions raised by both the parties and also to verify the genuineness of the documents relied by both the parties which could only be investigated after being sent to FSL.
8. Arguments heard.
Record perused.

sentences.text: 9. Impugned order was passed by Ld. Trial Court on 14.10.2023

Present revision petition was filed by complainant on 18.10.2023 which means that it was filed within limitation period and upon the application, stay was granted to the revisionist vide order dated 18.10.2023.
CR No. 625/2023 6 of 11 Kartar Singh Vs. Krishan & Ors.
10. The impugned order was not an interlocutory order.

That order decided the legal rights of the parties and therefore, present revision petition is maintainable before this court.
11.
The question which needs adjudication in present revision petition, is whether impugned order is perverse, illegal or arbitrary in nature ?

In order to decide said question, I have to refer to the record of Ld. Trial Court and the law governing application u/sec. 156(3) CrPC.
12.
Revisionist claimed that facts of this case did not require registration of FIR.
It is a settled principle of law that while deciding application u/sec. 156(3) CrPC, Ld. Magistrate is given discretion which he has to exercise after proper application of mind.
Further, the Magistrate should not order registration of FIR u/sec. 156(3) CrPC, without applying his mind, in a mechanical manner.

The powers u/sec. 156(3) CrPC, have to be exercised where the allegations are quite serious or evidence is beyond the reach of complainant or custodial interrogation appears to be necessary for recovery of some articles or discovery of facts.

13. For deciding the aforesaid question, it is relevant to mention here the relevant law governing the adjudication of application U/s. 156 (3) CrPC.
CR No. 625/2023 7 of 11 Kartar Singh Vs. Krishan & Ors.
14. Section 156 (3) CrPC reads as under:-
"156. Police officer's power to investigate cognizable case:-
(1) Any officer in charge of a police station may, without the order of a Magistrate,
investigate any cognizable case which a Court having jurisdiction over the local area within the limits of such station would have power to inquire into to try under the provisions of Chapter XIII.
Xxx xxx xxx (3) Any Magistrate empowered under Section 190 may order such an investigation as above- mentioned."

15. Section 156 (3) CrPC provides that a check by the Magistrate on the police performing its duty under Chapter 12 of CrPC, in cases where the Magistrate finds that the police has not done its duty,
investigating the case at all, or has not done it satisfactorily, he can issue a direction to the police to do the investigation properly and can monitor the same.
Reliance in this regard is placed upon case law titled as Dilawar Singh vs. State of Delhi (2007) 12 SCC 641.

sentences.text: In the case titled as Sukwasi vs. State of Uttar Pradesh [2008 Crl. LJ 472], it has been held that "Application under Section 156 (3) of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 are now coming in torrents.

entities.text: Sukwasi vs. State of Uttar Pradesh [2008 Crl. LJ 472]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Provisions under Section 156 (3) of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 CR No. 625/2023 8 of 11 Kartar Singh Vs. Krishan & Ors.
should be used sparingly.
They should not be used unless there is something unusual or extra ordinary like miscarriage of justice, which warrants a direction the police to register a case.

Such applications should not be allowed because the law provides them with an alternative remedy of filing a complaint, therefore, recourse should not normally be permitted for availing the provisions of section 156 (3) of Code of Criminal Procedure 1973.

The reference is, therefore, answered in the manner that it is not incumbent upon a Magistrate to allow an application under Section 156 (3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and there is no such legal mandate.
He may or may not allow the application in his discretion."

17. In the case titled as Ravindra Kumar vs. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr. [2013 VIII AD (Delhi) 403], it has been held that ;
"4. Section 156 (3) empowers the Magistrate to refer and direct the police to investigate the cognizable offence.

entities.text: Ravindra Kumar vs. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr. [2013 VIII AD (Delhi) 403]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It is however not necessary to refer every complaint filed under Section 200 to the police for investigation under Section 156 (3) of Cr.P.C.
Remedy under Section 156 (3) Cr.P.C. is a discretionary one as the provision proceeds with the word 'may'.

The Magistrate is required to exercise his mind while doing so and pass orders only if he is satisfied that the information reveals commission of cognizable offence/ CR No. 625/2023 9 of 11 Kartar Singh Vs. Krishan & Ors.
offences and also about necessity of police investigation for digging out of evidence neither in possession of the complainant nor can be procured without the assistance of the police.
The complainant, as a matter of right, cannot insist that the complaint case filed by him/her should be directed in every eventuality to the police for investigation."

18. In view of the said case laws, the issue which arises for adjudication is whether ld. Trial court has correctly or incorrectly used its judicial discretion, while rejecting application of complainant U/s.
156 (3) CrPC ?
19.
After going through the impugned order, I find that Ld. MM had not passed cryptic order.
The said impugned order has reasons, which are not repeated here for the sake of brevity.
Those reasons were outcome of proper exercise of judicial discretion.
The impugned order therefore was not arbitrary.
It was not perverse.

20. Further, Ld. Counsel for complainant argued that once cognizable offence is made out from the allegations of complaint, then u/sec. 156(3) Cr.PC, Ld. MM was left with no option but to order for investigation by allowing application of complainant.

In the same breath, in the grounds of revision,

sentences.text:
complainant averred that Ld. MM before exercising jurisdiction u/sec. 156(3) Cr.PC, was required to CR No. 625/2023 10 of 11 Kartar Singh Vs. Krishan & Ors.
apply his mind, which should be reflected in his order.
On the face of it, both the said stands are contradictory to each other.

On one hand, complainant alleged that after filing application u/sec.
156(3) Cr.PC., Ld. MM had no option but to order for investigation, which means that he was not required to apply his mind and on other hand, complainant averred that Ld. MM had to apply his mind on the contents of application u/sec. 156(3) Cr.PC.
The said contradictory stands of complainant did not help the cause of complainant.
It made the revision, meritless.
21. That order is a reasoned order and is not an arbitrary order, passed in a mechanical manner.
The impugned order is neither illegal nor perverse.
It needs no interference.
Accordingly, present revision petition, stands dismissed.
22. Stay stands vacated.
Concerned SHO is directed to register the FIR in relevant provisions of law within one week from today and the order of Ld. Trial Court dated 14.10.2023 is upheld.

23. Copy of this order be sent to SHO concerned for compliance.
24.
Copy of this judgment be also sent to the Ld. Trial Court for information and compliance.
